message:
QUESTION:
Did the 1 June move to a new content delivery network (CDN) improve the site's conversion rate, and what is a faster site worth?

DATA:
An online retailer migrated its website to a new content delivery network (CDN) on 1 June. Two weeks before (18-31 May) vs two weeks after (1-14 June):

| Metric | 18-31 May | 1-14 June |
| Sessions | 200,000 | 210,000 |
| Orders | 5,000 | 5,670 |
| Median page load time | 3.2 s | 2.1 s |
| 95th-percentile page load time | 7.5 s | 4.8 s |
| Bounce rate | 48% | 44% |

Conversion = orders / sessions. Page load times come from real-user monitoring across all page views.

Same two calendar periods last year, when there were no site or infrastructure changes: conversion 2.4% (18-31 May) and 2.6% (1-14 June).

The retailer's conversion rate rises every year in early June when the summer ranges launch. This year the summer ranges again launched on 1 June. No other site changes were made between 18 May and 14 June.

<analysis>
# CDN migration: performance and conversion impact

## Summary

- **The 1 June CDN migration made the site substantially faster.** Median load time fell 34% and 95th-percentile load time fell 36%. This gain can reasonably be credited to the CDN.
- **We did not detect a conversion gain from the migration.** Conversion rose from 2.50% to 2.70%. Over the same two weeks last year, with no site changes, it rose by the same amount, from 2.4% to 2.6%. Both years had the early-June summer-range launch.
- **That does not mean the CDN had no effect.** The comparison is too imprecise to tell. Our best estimate of the CDN's effect is about zero, but the plausible range is roughly **−0.25 to +0.25 points**. That range includes effects large enough to be commercially worthwhile.
- **We can't yet say what a faster site is worth.** Getting a reliable figure needs unrounded prior-year data, a revenue and traffic view, and ideally a controlled test.

## Background

- The site moved to a new CDN on 1 June. This note compares the two weeks before (18–31 May) with the two weeks after (1–14 June).
- Load times come from real-user monitoring (RUM) across all page views, so they reflect what customers actually experienced.
- The figures are site-wide totals. Device, channel, revenue and average order value are not included.
- No other site changes were made between 18 May and 14 June.
- The summer ranges launched on 1 June, as they do every year, and conversion always rises in early June. This is the main obstacle to measuring the CDN's effect: both changes happened on the same day.

## Speed

| Metric | 18–31 May | 1–14 June | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Median load time | 3.2 s | 2.1 s | −1.1 s (−34%) |
| 95th-percentile load time | 7.5 s | 4.8 s | −2.7 s (−36%) |

- The migration delivered a large, broad improvement. Both typical and slow page loads became about a third faster. The slowest loads saved the most time in absolute terms (2.7 s).
- A seasonal cause is very unlikely. If anything, higher summer traffic and heavier new-range pages would tend to slow the site, so the CDN's true gain may be slightly understated.
- One caveat: RUM averages over all page views. Lower bounce means visitors viewed a somewhat different mix of pages after the change. This has a small effect on the comparison but doesn't change the conclusion.

## Traffic and engagement

| Metric | 18–31 May | 1–14 June | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sessions | 200,000 | 210,000 | +5% |
| Orders | 5,000 | 5,670 | +13% |
| Orders per day | ~357 | 405 | +13% |
| Bounce rate | 48% | 44% | −4 pts (−8% relative) |

- All of these moved in the direction a faster site would produce. All of them are also likely to be lifted by the summer launch.
- We don't have last year's sessions, orders or bounce rate for these periods, so we can't separate the two causes for any of these metrics.

## Conversion

| | 18–31 May | 1–14 June | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| This year (CDN migration + summer launch) | 2.50% | 2.70% | +0.20 pts (+8.0%) |
| Last year (summer launch only) | 2.4% | 2.6% | +0.2 pts (+8.3%) |
| **Estimated CDN effect (difference)** | | | **≈ 0 pts** |

A simple before/after comparison would credit the CDN with +0.2 points, or about 420 extra orders a fortnight. That is misleading, because the same rise happened last year with no site changes. Netting off last year's seasonal rise leaves a central estimate of about zero.

This estimate is very uncertain, for three reasons.

### 1. Last year's figures are rounded
The figures 2.4% and 2.6% are given to one decimal place. Last year's true seasonal rise could therefore be anywhere from about 0.10 to 0.30 points.

- If last year was really 2.45% → 2.55%, the seasonal rise was only 0.1 points. The CDN could then account for about 0.1 points, or half of this year's rise.
- If last year was really 2.35% → 2.65%, the seasonal rise was 0.3 points. The CDN would then look slightly negative.
- Rounding alone therefore puts the estimated CDN effect anywhere between about −0.1 and +0.1 points.

### 2. Sampling noise
- Each two-week conversion rate carries a standard error of about 0.035 points.
- The comparison combines four rates: two this year and two last year. Assuming last year had similar volumes, this gives roughly **±0.14 points** at 95% confidence.
- This is a lower bound. It treats sessions as independent, but repeat visitors and multiple sessions per buyer add further noise.

### 3. The seasonal rise varies from year to year
We have only one prior year, so we can't estimate how much the early-June lift varies. Any variation adds further uncertainty on top of points 1 and 2.

### Combined uncertainty
Taken together, the CDN's effect on conversion plausibly lies somewhere between about **−0.25 and +0.25 points**, or roughly ±10% relative.

Industry figures for speed improvements are commonly in the range of a few percent of conversion per second saved. Those figures vary widely and are often poorly controlled themselves. For a 1.1-second gain at a 2.5% baseline, they imply roughly 0.05–0.2 points. That sits entirely inside our uncertainty range.

**Conclusion on conversion:** the data give no evidence that the CDN raised conversion. They also cannot rule out a commercially meaningful effect.

## Conversion rate may not capture the CDN's full value

- **Traffic.** Sessions rose 5%. A faster site can attract more sessions, for example through better search ranking or fewer abandoned visits. If the CDN brought in extra, lower-intent sessions, they would add orders while *diluting* the conversion rate.
- **Measurement.** With a 7.5-second 95th percentile before the migration, some visitors probably left before the analytics tag fired and were never counted as sessions. A faster site records more of these visitors, which inflates the session count. This could mask a real conversion gain.
- **Revenue.** "What is a faster site worth" is ultimately a revenue question. Average order value and revenue are not in these data. Faster pages could change basket size as well as the number of orders.

The right comparison is therefore sessions, orders and revenue growth against the same periods last year, not the conversion ratio alone.

## What is a faster site worth?

**We can't estimate this from these data.**

- An earlier figure of "0.18 points per second" was calculated as this year's 0.2-point conversion rise divided by the 1.1-second improvement in median load time.
- That figure attributes the seasonal rise to the CDN. It also assumes conversion responds in a straight line to load time, which may not hold beyond the range we observed.
- It should not be used in business cases.

To show what is at stake, here is a rough sizing. At current traffic, **each 0.1 points of conversion is worth about 210 orders a fortnight**, or roughly 5,000 orders a year if traffic held steady. Multiply by average order value and margin to get a money figure.

This gives a threshold for judging any future estimate. It also shows that effects too small for this comparison to detect could still be worth having.

## Next steps

1. **Get unrounded prior-year data.** Request last year's exact conversion, sessions, orders, revenue and bounce rate for both periods. This is the quickest way to narrow the estimate, and it costs nothing.
2. **Compare volumes and revenue against last year, not just conversion.** Check whether this year's growth in sessions, orders and revenue exceeds last year's seasonal growth.
3. **Strengthen the seasonal baseline.** Repeat the comparison using several prior years and daily data. This shows how much the early-June lift normally varies, and so how large a CDN effect we could detect.
4. **Look for a dose-response pattern.** Split the data by device, region and connection type, comparing each segment with the same segment last year. If conversion rose more where load times improved most, that is evidence of a real speed effect.
5. **Run a controlled test if a precise value is needed.** Options include routing a randomised share of traffic through the old delivery path (if still available) or adding latency to a random share of sessions. Two points to plan for:
   - **The test has a revenue cost.** Slowing the site for some customers will cost some sales, so keep the exposed share small.
   - **Small effects need a lot of traffic.** Detecting a 0.1-point effect needs roughly 400,000 sessions per group, about four weeks of total traffic split evenly. A small exposed share would take much longer. Testing a larger delay is faster but requires assuming the effect scales with delay. Agree the minimum effect worth detecting (see the sizing above) before designing the test.
6. **Keep monitoring load times** through the summer to confirm the speed gain holds as traffic grows.
7. **Don't use conversion uplift to justify further speed work until steps 1–5 give a credible estimate.** Performance work may still be justified on other grounds, such as user experience, search ranking or infrastructure cost.

## Conclusion

- The CDN migration cut median load time by 34% and 95th-percentile load time by 36%. This is a clear, attributable gain.
- Conversion rose by 0.2 points, but last year's seasonal rise was the same size. These data therefore give no evidence that the CDN added to conversion.
- Rounded prior-year figures, sampling noise and a single comparison year leave the CDN's effect anywhere between roughly −0.25 and +0.25 points. A commercially meaningful effect cannot be ruled out.
- Before valuing speed, get unrounded prior-year data and compare traffic and revenue as well as conversion. For a reliable figure, run a controlled test rather than a before/after comparison that overlaps the summer launch.
</analysis>

<review>
# Review: CDN migration analysis

The analysis is sound. Its central conclusion holds: the CDN clearly made the site faster, but these data can't show whether it raised conversion. I checked every figure. One calculation is wrong (the test duration), one range needs clearer labelling, and a few points could be tightened.

## Must fix

**1. The test duration is understated by about half (Next steps, item 5).**
"Roughly 400,000 sessions per group" is right. Detecting 0.1 points at a 2.5% baseline, with 5% two-sided significance and 80% power, needs about 380,000 per group. But two groups need about 800,000 sessions in total. At about 105,000 sessions a week, that takes **about 8 weeks**, not 4. Four weeks gives only about 420,000 sessions, which fills one group. Also state the significance and power assumptions so readers can rerun the sizing.

## Should fix

**2. The "combined uncertainty" range of ±0.25 isn't derived, and its heading overstates what it covers.**
- The ±0.25 looks like ±0.10 from rounding added directly to ±0.14 from sampling.
- Adding them directly overstates the spread. Rounding error behaves like a triangular distribution on ±0.10, with a standard deviation of about 0.04. Combining it with sampling properly gives about **±0.16 at 95%**.
- The third source, year-to-year variation in the seasonal rise, isn't included at all, because it can't be estimated from one prior year.
- The ±0.25 is a reasonable working figure, but say how it was built. It is a conservative combination of rounding and sampling, *excluding* year-to-year variation, so the true uncertainty could be wider. As written, "Taken together" implies all three sources are included.

**3. Add a relative-scale check of the seasonal adjustment.**
The adjustment assumes the seasonal lift adds the same number of points each year. It could instead scale with the baseline. On a relative basis, this year rose +8.0% and last year +8.3%, so the conclusion is the same. One sentence saying so would close an obvious reviewer question.

## Minor

**4. The annual order figure is slightly low.** 210 orders × 26 fortnights ≈ 5,500, not "roughly 5,000". Also, June traffic is seasonally high, so "if traffic held steady" at the June rate may overstate the annual figure. Say which traffic level you assumed.

**5. Bounce rate partly undercuts the session-measurement argument.** The analysis suggests the faster site now records visitors who used to leave before the analytics tag fired. Those newly recorded visitors would mostly be bounces, which should push the bounce rate *up*. Bounce actually fell from 48% to 44%. So either this effect is small, or the real improvement in engagement is larger than it looks. Either way, the point deserves a sentence. The argument should be presented as a possibility rather than a likely cause of masking.

**6. The "earlier figure of 0.18 points per second" has no context.** The arithmetic is correct (0.2 ÷ 1.1 ≈ 0.18). But readers who didn't see the earlier draft won't know where the figure came from. Say where it appeared, or explain it as "a naive estimate would give…".

**7. The industry benchmark has no source.** "A few percent of conversion per second" is fine as a rough guide, but cite a source or label it as an assumption. The resulting 0.05–0.2 point range checks out (about 2–7% per second × 1.1 s × 2.5%).

**8. Adding latency in a test may not mirror a speed gain.** Making the site slower may not have the mirror-image effect of making it faster. Mention this alongside the revenue-cost caveat.

## Verified as correct

- Conversion: 2.50% → 2.70% (+0.20 points, +8.0%). Last year +8.3%.
- Load times: median −1.1 s (−34%). 95th percentile −2.7 s (−36%).
- Bounce rate: −4 points (−8.3% relative). Orders per day: about 357 → 405.
- Rounding bounds: last year's seasonal rise could be 0.10–0.30 points, putting the CDN effect between −0.10 and +0.10.
- Standard error of each two-week rate: about 0.035 points. Four-rate comparison: about ±0.14 at 95%, assuming last year had similar volumes, which the analysis notes.
- 0.1 points of conversion ≈ 210 orders a fortnight.
- The reasoning against a seasonal cause for the speed gain, and the caveat about the mix of pages measured by real-user monitoring.

## Overall

Fix the test duration (item 1) and relabel the uncertainty range (item 2). Everything else is optional polish. The structure, caveats and next steps are well judged. Asking for unrounded prior-year data first is the right priority, because it costs nothing and directly narrows the largest identifiable source of uncertainty.
</review>

- It gives a threshold for judging any future estimate.
- It shows that effects too small for this comparison to detect could still be worth having.

1. **Get unrounded prior-year data.**
   - Request last year's exact conversion, sessions, orders, revenue and bounce rate for both periods.
   - This removes the rounding uncertainty at no cost, and is the quickest way to narrow the estimate.
2. **Compare volumes and revenue against last year, not just conversion.**
   - Check whether this year's growth in sessions, orders and revenue exceeds last year's seasonal growth.
3. **Strengthen the seasonal baseline.**
   - Repeat the comparison using several prior years and daily data.
   - This shows how much the early-June lift normally varies, and so how large a CDN effect we could detect.
4. **Look for a dose-response pattern.**
   - Split the data by device, region and connection type, comparing each segment with the same segment last year.
   - If conversion rose more where load times improved most, that is evidence of a real speed effect.
5. **Run a controlled test if a precise value is needed.**
   - Options include routing a randomised share of traffic through the old delivery path (if still available), or adding latency to a random share of sessions. Plan for three issues.
   - **Sample size and duration.**
     - Detecting a 0.1-point effect at a 2.5% baseline needs about 390,000 sessions per group, or about 780,000 in total. This assumes 5% two-sided significance and 80% power.

     - A 10% exposed share would need about 2.2 million sessions in total, roughly **20 weeks**.
     - Non-independent sessions would lengthen both.
     - Agree the minimum effect worth detecting (see the sizing above) before designing the test.
   - **Revenue cost.**
     - Slowing the site for some customers will cost some sales.
     - This must be balanced against the longer duration a small exposed share requires.
   - **Asymmetry.**
     - Customers may react more strongly to a site getting slower than to one getting faster, so adding latency may overstate the value of speed.
     - Testing a larger delay finishes sooner, but assumes the effect scales with the delay. Both assumptions should be stated alongside any result.
6. **Keep monitoring load times** through the summer to confirm the speed gain holds as traffic grows.
7. **Don't use conversion uplift to justify further speed work until steps 1–5 give a credible estimate.**
   - Performance work may still be justified on other grounds, such as user experience, search ranking or infrastructure cost.

## Conclusion

- **The CDN made the site clearly faster.** Median load time fell 34% and 95th-percentile load time fell 36%.
- **There is no evidence it raised conversion.** Conversion rose 0.2 points, but last year's seasonal rise was the same size, whether measured in points or percentages.
- **A meaningful effect cannot be ruled out.**
  - Rounding and sampling noise alone leave a range of about ±0.16 points.
  - Year-to-year variation in the seasonal rise widens it further, to roughly ±0.25 as a working allowance.
- **Before valuing speed:**
  - Get unrounded prior-year data.
  - Compare traffic and revenue as well as conversion.
  - For a reliable figure, run a controlled test of about 8 weeks, rather than a before/after comparison that overlaps the summer launch.
